Public Money · CRA Spending Where Bay County's CRA money goes Every Community Redevelopment Agency in Bay County, mapped on the county's official district boundaries, with the payments, grants, contracts and budget lines found in public records: who got paid, where, and for what. Export PDF Data updated Oct 24, 2026 Six CRAs · 14 districts City All six CRAs Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker The simple version What's a CRA? A Community Redevelopment Agency is like a savings jar for one neighborhood that needs fixing up. Take a snapshot. When the CRA starts, the city writes down what all the property inside its district is worth. That's the base year . Watch it grow. As buildings get fixed up and new ones go up, the area becomes worth more. The growth fills the jar. Property tax on that extra value, the tax increment , goes into the CRA's trust fund instead of the city's and county's main budgets. It can only be spent on that neighborhood, until the CRA's end date . Why it matters: every dollar in the jar is a dollar the city and county don't have for everything else. This page shows what each jar paid for. The Property Appraiser sets it each January. Subtract any homestead exemption and you get your taxable value . Each government picks a rate. The county, the school board, your city and a few special districts each set a rate in mills . One mill is $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. Add up the slices. Public Money · Amendment 3 Amendment 3: what changes in Bay County if it passes On November 3, 2026, Florida voters decide Amendment 3, a property tax change. It needs at least 60% "yes" to pass. This page shows what it would do to your bill and to local budgets here, using the state's own estimates. BayCounty.me takes no position on Amendment 3. Arguments on both sides are summarized below, with sources. Export PDF Data updated Oct 20, 2026 The simple version What Amendment 3 does A much bigger discount for homeowners. Today a homestead gets about $50,000 knocked off its value for city, county and special-district taxes. Amendment 3 raises that to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 , then grows it with inflation. School taxes don't change. Homeowners still get only the first $25,000 off for school taxes, so almost everyone keeps paying those. New Floridians wait. People who weren't Florida residents on December 31, 2026 get a $50,000 discount for their first four years, then the bigger one. Slower growth for everyone else. For rentals, businesses, second homes and land, the yearly limit on how fast the taxed value can rise drops from 10% to 5% (not for school taxes). Limits on what property tax can pay for. Cities and counties could spend it only on listed things such as public safety, schools, infrastructure, natural resources, debt and pensions, and running government. It takes effect January 1, 2027. The first bills affected would be the ones mailed in November 2027. The amendment also tells the Legislature to set up a way for cities and counties to go further and exempt homesteads completely. Public Money · Hurricane Michael Where the Hurricane Michael money went Hurricane Michael hit Bay County on October 10, 2018. Billions in federal, state and insurance money followed. This page tracks the public part: who received it, what it paid for, and what's still unclear. Export PDF FEMA data refreshed Oct 20, 2026 Data updated Oct 23, 2026 Government All governments Bay County Bay District Schools Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach The simple version How disaster money works FEMA pays governments back. After a disaster declaration, FEMA's Public Assistance program reimburses cities, the county, schools and some nonprofits for debris cleanup, emergency work and rebuilding public buildings. Each job is a "project" with its own paperwork. FEMA helps households. Individual Assistance gives grants to homeowners and renters for repairs, temporary rent and other needs. HUD funds the long rebuild. Congress later sent Florida disaster block grants (CDBG-DR), which the state handed out through "Rebuild Florida" for housing, infrastructure and downtowns. Loans and insurance fill in. SBA disaster loans and flood insurance claims went straight to residents and businesses. Public Money · Sales Tax Projects The half-cent sales taxes: what was promised, what got built Bay County has two extra half-cent sales taxes that voters approved: one for roads and infrastructure, one for school buildings. Here is every infrastructure project on the county's map, and what we could find about the school tax. Export PDF Data updated Oct 23, 2026 Government All governments Bay County Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach The school half-cent is countywide The simple version How the half-cent taxes work Everyone who shops here pays. Each adds half a cent to every dollar of taxable purchases in Bay County, including purchases by tourists. Voters set the rules. The infrastructure tax started January 2017 and voters extended it in November 2024 through 2036. The school tax runs through 2030. It can only build things. The infrastructure money goes to roads, bridges, dirt-road paving, drainage and safety projects. The school money goes to school construction, renovation, security and technology. The county and cities split the infrastructure tax by a state formula based on population. Non-ad valorem assessments charge per home, per parcel or by building size for a specific service, like fire protection or stormwater drainage. Learn and reuse · API BayCounty.me API Connect your own app, spreadsheet, newsroom tool or AI assistant to the public records on this site. Free, read-only, and no key needed. Open the API 60 datasets Quick start Endpoints Filtering Datasets API keys AI assistants (MCP) Use and limits Quick start Every dataset on the Open data page is also available as an API. Responses are JSON (or CSV with format=csv ), and every row carries a link to its source record. Rows are served live from the BayCounty.me database, so newly added records show up within about five minutes; each response says where its rows came from in meta.data_source . curl 'https://baycounty.me/api/v1/datasets/contracts?government=Bay%20County%20BOCC&amount_min=1000000&sort=-amount&limit=5' curl 'https://baycounty.me/api/v1/datasets/votes?board=Lynn%20Haven%20City%20Commission&split=true&date_from=2025-01-01' curl 'https://baycounty.me/api/v1/datasets/salary-positions?category=law_enforcement&fields=employer,title,pay_min,pay_max&format=csv' Base URL: https://baycounty.me/api/v1 · Machine-readable description: OpenAPI 3.1 (import it into Postman, a GPT action, or any OpenAPI tool). Endpoints Request Returns GET /api/v1 Index: every dataset with row counts and links GET /api/v1/datasets Catalog with every column, its type and, for short lists, its allowed values GET /api/v1/datasets/{id} Rows: {data: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset, next}} GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}/schema Columns and types for one dataset GET /api/v1/governments A profile of each local government: budget, tax rate, debt, audits, votes, staff GET /api/v1/governments/{slug} One profile, with years : budget, tax rate, audited actuals, residents, debt and staff for each fiscal year on record. E.g. lynn-haven GET /api/v1/status Rows in each dataset, when the database last loaded it, and any load errors GET /api/v1/changes?since= Records added since a date or time, e.g. new contracts since Oct. 1 . Add dataset= to pick datasets GET /api/v1/meetings.ics?gov= Calendar feed of upcoming meetings for one government, e.g. Lynn Haven . Keys: county, schools, pc, pcb, lh, cw, sp, parker, mb; a board such as lh-cra works too, and commas combine them. Paste the link into Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar ("subscribe by URL"). Every board at once: /meetings.ics GET /api/v1/correspondence?year= Published letters BayCounty.me sent to officials, with their replies, e.g. every year . Add government= for one government. Only threads approved for publication are included GET /api/v1/pages Which datasets and endpoints hold the data behind each page on the site, e.g. the Connections network GET /api/v1/entities?q= Find a company, official, candidate, nonprofit, board member, business or government by name, e.g. dewberry . Add kind= (gov, vendor, person, nonprofit, member, business, committee) GET /api/v1/entities/{id} One profile and every documented connection: payments, contracts, campaign gifts from organizations, votes, board seats, businesses and grants, each with its source, e.g. vendor:dewberry . Officials' board seats and businesses appear once an editor checks the match GET /api/v1/search?q= Search every page on the site, e.g. martin theatre GET /downloads/{id}.json The whole dataset as one file, for bulk use Filtering, sorting and paging Match a column: ?government=City%20of%20Callaway (spaces as %20 ; the catalog lists each column's allowed values). Matching ignores capitals. Separate several values with commas to match any of them: ?outcome=failed,tabled . Ranges: add _min or _max to a number column ( amount_min=500000 ) and _from or _to to a date ( date_from=2025-10-01 ). Text: _contains on a column ( vendor_contains=roberts ), or q= to search every column. Not equal: _ne leaves out values ( outcome_ne=passed ; commas for several). Empty or not: _null=true finds rows where a column is blank, _null=false rows where it has a value ( amount_null=false ). Blank values never match _min , _max , _from or _to . Totals: group_by=government&sum=amount returns one row per group with count , sum_amount and n_amount (how many numbers were added), largest group first. Filters apply first, and it works with format=csv . Example: contract dollars by government . Sort: sort=-amount,date (a minus sign sorts high to low). Columns: fields=vendor,amount,source_url . Paging: limit (up to 1,000, default 100) and offset . The response's meta.next is the link to the next page. Caching: responses carry an ETag (and Last-Modified where the data's date is known). Send it back as If-None-Match (or If-Modified-Since ) and you get 304 Not Modified with no body when nothing changed. Send a key in any of these ways (the header is best, so the key stays out of logs and browser history): curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer bcm_your_key' 'https://baycounty.me/api/v1/datasets/votes?limit=5' Authorization: Bearer <key> or X-API-Key: <key> header, or ?api_key=<key> on the URL. The MCP server takes the same header. Every response carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining (per minute), plus X-RateLimit-Limit-Day and X-RateLimit-Remaining-Day when a daily limit applies. Daily limits reset at midnight Central time. Over a limit, you get status 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds. A wrong key gets 401 ; a paused, revoked or expired key gets 403 . Connect an AI assistant (MCP) BayCounty.me runs a Model Context Protocol server, so AI assistants that support remote MCP servers can look up these records directly and cite them. There's no sign-in. https://baycounty.me/api/mcp Claude: add a custom connector and paste the address above. Other assistants and tools: add it as a remote MCP server using the "Streamable HTTP" transport. Tools it offers: list_datasets , query_dataset , get_government , search_site , upcoming_meetings (by government, days ahead or a keyword such as a street name), member_voting_record (one board member's votes, including when they were in the minority) and vendor_profile (one company's contracts, change orders, payments, CRA payments and business campaign contributions; a match doesn't show why anything happened) and official_correspondence (published letters to officials and their replies), and find_entity and get_entity (anyone or anything on the site and every documented connection: who paid it, campaign gifts from organizations, votes, board seats and businesses). Resources: each dataset is also an MCP resource at baycounty://datasets/<id> (up to 2,000 rows; the full file is linked). Example question: "Which Bay County contracts over $5 million went to campaign donors, and how did commissioners vote?" Use and limits The data is compiled from public records and free to reuse. Please credit BayCounty.me and link to the source record for any figure you publish. Check the original record before relying on a single number. Each dataset's notes and gaps are on its page on this site. Individual campaign donors and rank-and-file public employees are not named, here or anywhere on the site. Each API and MCP request is logged with its time, query, key (if any) and IP address, to enforce limits and stop abuse. IP addresses are deleted from the log after 90 days. Requests are limited per connection or per key (see API keys ). For bulk use, download the full files from /downloads . Data refreshes as the site updates, and meetings and campaign reports refresh every morning. Questions or a use you'd like supported? Get in touch .

Mi dirección Lo que aplica a su dirección Escriba una dirección del Condado de Bay para ver el cálculo aproximado de su impuesto a la propiedad, quién lo representa, sus escuelas, sus zonas de inundación y de evacuación, y si está dentro de un distrito de reurbanización. Dirección Empiece con el número de la casa. Las búsquedas van directamente al servidor público de mapas del Condado de Bay; BayCounty.me no guarda lo que usted busca. Exportar PDF Registro del Tasador de Propiedades ↗ Cálculo aproximado del impuesto a la propiedad La propiedad Si se aprueba la Enmienda 3 (Amendment 3) Quién lo representa Escuelas públicas asignadas Distrito de reurbanización ( CRA ) Inundaciones, tormentas y servicios Zonificación y desarrollo cercanos Dinero público cerca de usted Los registros de su gobierno Aquí no se muestran los nombres de los dueños. Son públicos en el sitio del Tasador de Propiedades (Property Appraiser), enlazado arriba. Los nombres de los representantes vienen del GIS del Condado de Bay y pueden tardar en actualizarse después de una elección. Los nombres de agencias, distritos y escuelas aparecen como los publica el condado, en inglés. Los enlaces a otras secciones llevan al sitio en inglés. Cómo funciona Las direcciones, las parcelas, los valores de las propiedades y los límites de los distritos se consultan en vivo en el servidor público de GIS del Condado de Bay , que publica los datos de parcelas del Tasador de Propiedades. Los valores de las propiedades son los del registro de 2026. Las zonas de inundación se consultan en vivo en la Capa Nacional de Riesgo de Inundación de FEMA (National Flood Hazard Layer) , el mapa oficial de inundaciones vigente, con el panel FIRM y cualquier revisión del mapa (LOMR) que corresponda. El cálculo de impuestos aplica el conjunto completo más reciente de tasas oficiales (año tributario 2025, facturas del FY2026, del Departamento de Ingresos de Florida [Florida Department of Revenue]) a los valores de 2026. Las tasas adoptadas en septiembre de 2026 las reemplazarán cuando el estado publique el conjunto completo. Las tarifas fijas no basadas en el valor (non-ad valorem) (bomberos, aguas pluviales, alumbrado y similares) vienen del archivo por parcela del Departamento de Ingresos de Florida para el registro tributario de 2025, así que muestran lo que había en la factura del FY2026. Para una vivienda con homestead, el impuesto escolar se calcula sobre el valor antes de la segunda exención de homestead, ya que esa no se aplica a las escuelas. Las demás exenciones se toman tal como las informa el Tasador de Propiedades. Su factura oficial la envía el Recaudador de Impuestos (Tax Collector).

Glosario Guía en lenguaje sencillo El dinero público viene con mucha jerga. Aquí está cada término de este sitio, explicado primero de forma sencilla y luego con más detalle. En todo el sitio, una palabra con subrayado punteado se puede tocar para ver su explicación corta. Agencias de Reurbanización Comunitaria (CRA) Impuestos a la propiedad y su factura Presupuestos y de dónde viene el dinero Cómo clasificamos el gasto en este sitio Contratos, terrenos y préstamos Registros públicos Elecciones y reuniones Agencias de Reurbanización Comunitaria (CRA) Agencia de Reurbanización Comunitaria (Community Redevelopment Agency, CRA) Una alcancía para un vecindario que necesita mejoras. Cuando las propiedades del vecindario aumentan de valor, el dinero adicional de impuestos va a la alcancía, y solo se puede gastar en ese vecindario. La ley de Florida permite que una ciudad o un condado cree una CRA para una zona que declara oficialmente deteriorada. Normalmente, la comisión de la ciudad funciona como la junta directiva de la CRA. La CRA sigue un plan de reurbanización por escrito y tiene una fecha de terminación. Ejemplo: La CRA de Lynn Haven abarca unos 695 acres alrededor de las avenidas Ohio y Florida. Distrito de la CRA (CRA district) La línea dibujada en el mapa alrededor del vecindario que cubre una CRA. El dinero que se recauda dentro de la línea se gasta dentro de la línea. Algunas CRA tienen varios distritos. Panama City tiene cuatro: Downtown, Downtown North, St. Andrews y Millville. Incremento de impuestos (tax increment, TIF) El impuesto a la propiedad adicional que genera un vecindario porque sus propiedades valen más desde que empezó la CRA. Ese adicional es lo que llena la alcancía de la CRA. El día en que empieza una CRA, se anota el valor total de las propiedades dentro de ella. Cada año después, la ciudad y el condado pagan al fondo fiduciario de la CRA los impuestos sobre cualquier valor por encima de esa cifra inicial. TIF son las siglas en inglés de "tax increment financing" (financiamiento por incremento de impuestos). Ejemplo: Si un distrito valía $100 millones cuando empezó y ahora vale $150 millones, los impuestos sobre la diferencia de $50 millones van a la CRA. Año base (base year) La foto inicial de cuánto valían todas las propiedades de una CRA. Solo el crecimiento por encima de esa cifra aporta dinero a la CRA. El año base se fija cuando se crea la CRA y no cambia durante toda la vida de la CRA. Fondo fiduciario de la CRA (CRA trust fund) La cuenta bancaria propia de la CRA. Ahí entra el incremento de impuestos y, por ley, solo se puede gastar en el plan de esa CRA. La ley estatal (Capítulo 163, Parte III) exige que cada CRA mantenga su dinero en un fondo fiduciario separado y que informe cada año cómo lo gastó. Fecha de terminación (sunset date) El día en que está previsto que termine una CRA. Después de esa fecha, el dinero adicional de impuestos vuelve a los presupuestos de la ciudad y del condado. Una ciudad puede votar para extender la vida de una CRA. Lynn Haven extendió su CRA hasta 2043 en enero de 2026. Reembolso de TIF (TIF rebate) Un acuerdo en el que la CRA le devuelve a un constructor parte de los nuevos impuestos que genera su proyecto, durante un número fijo de años, para ayudar a que el proyecto se construya. El reembolso se paga solo después de que el dueño paga la factura de impuestos completa, y tiene un monto máximo. Ejemplo: Panama City aprobó cinco reembolsos de TIF en el centro en diciembre de 2024. Subvención para fachadas (façade or storefront grant) Dinero que una CRA le da al dueño de un negocio para arreglar el frente de su edificio, por lo general igualando lo que gasta el dueño. La mayoría de los programas son 50/50: la CRA paga la mitad, hasta un límite, después de que se termina la obra. Impuestos a la propiedad y su factura Impuesto a la propiedad (ad valorem tax) Un impuesto basado en lo que vale su casa o terreno. Las propiedades de más valor pagan más. Ad valorem es latín y significa "según el valor". Varios gobiernos cobran cada uno su propio impuesto a la propiedad, y todos aparecen en una sola factura del Recaudador de Impuestos (Tax Collector). Autoridad tributaria (taxing authority) Cualquier gobierno autorizado para poner un impuesto a la propiedad en su factura, como el condado, la junta escolar o su ciudad. Cada una fija su propia tasa cada año en una audiencia pública. Tasa en milésimas (millage, mills) La forma en que se escriben las tasas del impuesto a la propiedad. Un "mill" significa $1 de impuesto por cada $1,000 del valor sobre el que se cobra impuesto a su propiedad. Una tasa de 5.5 mills equivale a 0.55%. Su factura suma los mills de cada autoridad tributaria que cubre su dirección. Ejemplo: 5 mills sobre una casa con un valor gravable de $200,000 son $1,000 al año. Valor justo (just value) El cálculo del Tasador de Propiedades (Property Appraiser) de lo que su propiedad se vendería. Se fija con fecha del 1 de enero de cada año. Valor tasado (assessed value) El valor de su propiedad después de aplicar los límites a qué tan rápido puede subir. Para una vivienda principal con exención de homestead, normalmente sube más despacio que el mercado. La regla Save Our Homes de Florida impide que el valor tasado de una vivienda con homestead suba más de 3% al año, o la tasa de inflación si es menor. Valor gravable (taxable value) La cifra sobre la que realmente se calcula su impuesto: el valor tasado menos cualquier exención. Puede ser distinta para los impuestos escolares y los demás impuestos, porque una de las exenciones de homestead no se aplica a los impuestos escolares. Exención de vivienda principal (homestead exemption) Un descuento en los impuestos a la propiedad para la casa donde usted vive todo el año, siempre que lo solicite. Los primeros $25,000 de valor están exentos de todos los impuestos a la propiedad. Una segunda cantidad, sobre el valor tasado por encima de $50,000, está exenta de todos los impuestos excepto los escolares. Era de $25,000 hasta 2024 y ahora sube con la inflación: $25,722 en 2025 y $26,411 en 2026. Ejemplo: En 2025, a una vivienda con homestead y un valor tasado de $200,000 la ciudad y el condado le cobraban impuestos sobre $149,278, y la junta escolar sobre $175,000. Tasa de reversión (rolled-back rate) La tasa de impuestos que recaudaría el mismo dinero que el año pasado de las mismas propiedades. Si un gobierno escoge una tasa más alta, la ley lo llama un aumento de impuestos, aunque la tasa no haya cambiado. Las construcciones nuevas no se incluyen en el cálculo, así que el crecimiento por sí solo no cuenta como aumento. Aviso TRIM (TRIM notice) La tarjeta postal que usted recibe cada agosto con sus impuestos propuestos y las fechas de las audiencias públicas. TRIM son las siglas en inglés de "Truth in Millage" (Veracidad en las Tasas), la ley de Florida que fija los pasos que los gobiernos deben seguir antes de subir los impuestos a la propiedad. Cargo no basado en el valor (non-ad valorem assessment) Una tarifa fija en su factura de impuestos por un servicio, como la recolección de basura o la protección contra incendios. No se basa en lo que vale su propiedad. Aparece en la misma factura que los impuestos a la propiedad, pero se calcula por vivienda, por acre o por unidad en lugar de por valor. MSTU Una zona de impuesto adicional del condado que paga servicios en solo una parte del condado, por lo general las zonas fuera de las ciudades. MSTU son las siglas en inglés de "Municipal Service Taxing Unit" (Unidad Tributaria de Servicios Municipales). Aporte Local Obligatorio (Required Local Effort) La tasa de impuesto escolar que el estado le indica a cada distrito escolar que cobre para poder recibir su parte del dinero estatal para escuelas. La Legislatura la fija cada año. Las juntas escolares pueden agregar una pequeña tasa discrecional y una tasa de capital para edificios. Límite Save Our Homes (Save Our Homes cap) Un límite a qué tan rápido puede subir el valor gravado de una vivienda con homestead: 3% al año, o menos si la inflación es menor. Las propiedades de alquiler, los negocios y las segundas viviendas tienen un límite más amplio de 10%. Los límites se aplican al valor tasado, no a las tasas de impuestos. La Enmienda 3 (Amendment 3) bajaría el límite de 10% a 5% para los impuestos no escolares. Gravamen (levy) El total de impuesto a la propiedad que un gobierno recauda en un año: su tasa multiplicada por todo el valor gravable de su zona. Exención (exemption) Una parte del valor de su propiedad sobre la que no paga impuesto. Si tiene una exención de $25,000, le cobran como si su casa valiera $25,000 menos. Casi todas las exenciones las fija la Constitución de Florida. Hay que pedirlas al Tasador de Propiedades (Property Appraiser), por lo general antes del 1 de marzo. Algunas son para veteranos, personas mayores con ingresos bajos o personas con discapacidad. Ejemplo: Una casa tasada en $200,000 con la exención de homestead paga impuesto de la ciudad y del condado sobre unos $150,000. Aguas pluviales (stormwater) El agua de lluvia que corre por las calles y los techos. Las ciudades y el condado cobran una tarifa para pagar las zanjas, los tubos y los estanques que la llevan. La tarifa de aguas pluviales casi siempre es fija por casa o por parcela y aparece en la factura de impuestos o en la factura de servicios. Presupuestos y de dónde viene el dinero Conferencia de Estimación de Ingresos (Revenue Estimating Conference) El equipo de economistas del estado que calcula cuánto dinero sumaría o restaría una nueva ley o enmienda. Personal de la Legislatura, de la oficina del Gobernador y de la Oficina de Investigación Económica y Demográfica (Office of Economic and Demographic Research) acuerdan una sola estimación oficial. Ejemplo: Para la Enmienda 3, calculó la pérdida de cada condado, ciudad y distrito especial. Año fiscal (fiscal year, FY) El año de presupuesto de un gobierno. En Florida va del 1 de octubre al 30 de septiembre. Lleva el nombre del año en que termina. Ejemplo: El FY2026 va del 1 de octubre de 2025 al 30 de septiembre de 2026. Fondo general (general fund) La cuenta corriente principal de un gobierno para los servicios de todos los días, como la policía, los parques y el funcionamiento del ayuntamiento. La mayor parte del impuesto a la propiedad va aquí. El dinero para fines especiales se guarda en fondos separados. Fondo empresarial (enterprise fund) Una cuenta para un servicio que usted paga directamente, como el agua y el alcantarillado. Las facturas que usted paga cubren el servicio. Funcionan como un pequeño negocio dentro del gobierno. Fondo de ingresos especiales (special revenue fund) Dinero que por ley solo se puede gastar en una cosa, como el impuesto a la gasolina para carreteras o el fondo fiduciario de una CRA. Ingresos compartidos del estado (state shared revenue) Dinero que el estado recauda, sobre todo del impuesto sobre las ventas, y devuelve a las ciudades y los condados. La parte más grande es el programa del medio centavo del impuesto sobre las ventas. Las ciudades y los condados también reciben dinero de reparto de ingresos según su población y otros factores. Cobros por servicios (charges for services) Dinero que un gobierno gana cobrando por cosas que ofrece, como las facturas de agua, la recolección de basura, los permisos y las tarifas de los parques. Ingresos intergubernamentales (intergovernmental revenue) Dinero que un gobierno recibe de otro, como subvenciones federales o ingresos compartidos del estado. Funcionarios constitucionales (constitutional officers) Los funcionarios electos del condado que nombra la constitución de Florida: el alguacil (sheriff), el tasador de propiedades, el recaudador de impuestos, el secretario del tribunal (clerk of court) y el supervisor de elecciones. Cada uno tiene su propio presupuesto, y el condado paga la mayor parte de ellos. Auditoría / informe financiero anual (audit / annual financial report) Una revisión anual de las cuentas de un gobierno hecha por contadores externos, para asegurarse de que los números cuadran y de que se siguieron las reglas. Los gobiernos de Florida deben presentar sus auditorías e informes financieros ante el estado. Este sitio usa esos documentos. Cómo clasificamos el gasto en este sitio Gastado (Spent) El registro indica que el dinero realmente se pagó. Comprometido (Committed) Se aprobó un contrato o una adjudicación, pero todavía no se ha pagado todo el dinero. Presupuestado (Budgeted) Dinero apartado en un plan. Puede que se gaste o puede que no. Propuesto (Proposed) Una idea o solicitud que no se ha aprobado. Excluido de los totales (Left out of totals) Se muestra en el sitio, pero no se suma a los totales, para que el mismo dólar nunca se cuente dos veces. Ejemplos: una orden de cambio que ya forma parte del total de un proyecto, un posible duplicado o dinero que no viene de la CRA. Contratos, terrenos y préstamos Orden de cambio (change order) Un cambio aprobado a un contrato después de firmado, que a menudo agrega costo o tiempo. Derecho de vía (right-of-way) El terreno donde está una carretera más la franja a su lado para aceras, servicios públicos y drenaje. Ampliar una carretera a menudo significa comprar más derecho de vía. Expropiación (eminent domain) Cuando un gobierno compra un terreno privado para un proyecto público aunque el dueño no quiera vender. Un tribunal decide el precio justo. El proceso judicial se llama "condemnation" (expropiación forzosa). Bono (bond) Una forma en que un gobierno pide dinero prestado ahora y lo devuelve con intereses durante muchos años, como una hipoteca. Los pagos anuales se llaman servicio de la deuda (debt service). Distrito de Desarrollo Comunitario (Community Development District, CDD) Un gobierno especial creado para un solo desarrollo, para construir y pagar sus calles, tuberías y otros servicios básicos. Los dueños de las propiedades de ahí lo pagan. Acuerdo interlocal (interlocal agreement) Un contrato entre dos gobiernos, como una ciudad y el condado. Registros públicos Solicitud de registros públicos (public records request) Pedirle a un gobierno que le muestre o le envíe sus registros. En Florida, cualquier persona puede pedirlos, y no tiene que decir por qué. La ley de registros públicos de Florida es el Capítulo 119 de los Estatutos de Florida. Los gobiernos pueden cobrar por las copias y por grandes cantidades de tiempo del personal. Registro de pagos (check register) La lista de un gobierno de cada pago que hizo: a quién se le pagó, cuánto, cuándo y por qué. Es la forma más directa de ver adónde fue el dinero, y la mayoría de las ciudades no lo publican en internet. Elecciones y reuniones Calificar como candidato (qualifying) El paso en que un candidato entrega sus papeles y paga la cuota, o junta firmas, para aparecer en la boleta. Si no lo hace a tiempo, no aparece. Cada elección tiene una semana de inscripción que fija la ley. Si solo una persona califica para un puesto, gana sin oposición y el puesto no aparece en la boleta. Donación en especie (in-kind contribution) Una donación a una campaña que no es dinero, sino cosas o servicios, como comida para un evento o letreros gratis. La ley de Florida cuenta las donaciones en especie igual que las de dinero, con el mismo límite por persona o negocio. Elección revocatoria (recall election) Una votación para decidir si un funcionario electo sale de su cargo antes de que termine su período. En Florida, los votantes de una ciudad pueden pedirla juntando firmas. Si el funcionario renuncia antes, la votación se cancela. Comentario público (public comment) El momento de una reunión del gobierno en que cualquier persona puede hablar a la junta, casi siempre por unos 3 minutos. La ley de Florida da al público el derecho a hablar antes de que una junta vote sobre la mayoría de los temas. La agenda dice cómo y cuándo pedir la palabra.

Participe Solicite un registro público La ley de registros públicos de Florida permite que cualquier persona vea los registros del gobierno. No tiene que explicar por qué. Elija un gobierno y un registro, o describa el suyo, y nosotros escribimos la solicitud. La carta se escribe en inglés. Así la oficina la puede atender sin demora. Abajo de la carta está lo que dice, en español. También puede pedir los registros en persona o por teléfono, en el idioma que prefiera. 1. Gobierno 2. ¿Qué registro quiere? Descripción de los registros (va en la carta, en inglés) Su nombre Su correo electrónico Teléfono (opcional) Muchas solicitudes tienen un cargo por copias o por tiempo del personal. Su nombre y su correo le permiten a la oficina enviarle un estimado de costos y los registros. Pedir copias electrónicas Su solicitud (en inglés) Copiar Abrir en el correo Abrir el portal de registros Imprimir Qué dice la carta, en español Fecha. Para: el encargado de registros del gobierno elegido. Asunto: solicitud de registros públicos. "Conforme a la Ley de Registros Públicos de Florida, Capítulo 119 de los Estatutos de Florida, solicito copias de los siguientes registros públicos: [su descripción]. Por favor, entréguelos en formato electrónico (PDF o el formato original, como Excel) por correo si es posible. Si alguna parte está exenta, cite la exención específica de cada parte retenida y entregue el resto, como exige la sección 119.07(1)(e) y (f). Si la solicitud implica un cargo por servicio especial o costos de copias de más de $25, envíeme un estimado antes de proceder. Preparé esta solicitud con la herramienta gratuita de BayCounty.me, un sitio independiente de registros públicos. BayCounty.me no hace esta solicitud y no necesita una copia. Envíe todas las respuestas, estimados y registros directamente a mí, a los datos de contacto de abajo. Gracias por su ayuda." Y su nombre, su correo y, si lo dio, su teléfono. Bueno saber Cualquier persona puede pedir. Según el Capítulo 119 de los Estatutos de Florida, puede pedir registros en persona, por teléfono, por correo electrónico o por carta, y no tiene que explicar por qué. La ley no exige su nombre, pero cuando hay un cargo la oficina necesita cómo enviarle el estimado, cobrar y entregarle los registros, así que este formulario lo incluye. Costos. Las agencias pueden cobrar por las copias (normalmente 15 centavos por página) y, si la solicitud requiere mucho tiempo del personal, un cargo por servicio especial. La carta dice que se preparó en BayCounty.me, pero pide que todas las respuestas, estimados y registros se le envíen directamente a usted. BayCounty.me no recibe nada. Esta página escribe la solicitud; no la envía ni guarda una copia. Nada de lo que escribe aquí se guarda.

Lo fija el Tasador de Propiedades (Property Appraiser) cada enero. Réstele cualquier exención de vivienda principal (homestead) y le queda su valor gravable . Cada gobierno escoge una tasa. El condado, la junta escolar, su ciudad y algunos distritos especiales fijan cada uno una tasa en milésimas (mills) . Una milésima es $1 por cada $1,000 de valor gravable. Se suman las partes. Su factura es cada tasa multiplicada por su valor gravable. El Recaudador de Impuestos (Tax Collector) envía una sola factura y le pasa a cada gobierno la parte que le toca. Cada uno de estos gobiernos es una autoridad tributaria . Las tasas de esta página son del año fiscal FY2026. Una exención de $25,000 quiere decir que le cobran como si su casa valiera $25,000 menos. Una exención completa quiere decir que no paga nada de impuesto a la propiedad. Casi todas las fija la Constitución de Florida y la ley del estado. Los gobiernos locales solo escogen unas pocas, como la exención adicional para personas mayores con ingresos bajos. El valor exento reparte el costo. Cuando un valor está exento, cada tasa cobra menos sobre él, así que el resto de las propiedades carga más del presupuesto. Portal de datos del DOR de Florida "Impuesto que se quita" aplica el último conjunto completo de tasas aprobadas (facturas del FY2026, las mismas tasas que usa Mi dirección) al valor que quita cada exención, parcela por parcela, con el distrito tributario de cada parcela. Si una parcela tiene varias exenciones, el impuesto se reparte entre ellas según la cantidad. No incluye el límite Save Our Homes , que frena qué tan rápido sube el valor gravado de una vivienda con homestead y no es una exención. Get involved Request a public record Florida's public records law lets anyone see government records, without saying why. Pick a government and a record this site is missing, or describe your own, and we'll write the request for you. 1. Government 2. What do you want? Describe the records Your name Your email Phone (optional) Many requests carry a copying or staff-time charge. Your name and email let the office send you a cost estimate and the records. Ask for electronic copies Your request Copy Open in email Open records portal Print Good to know Anyone can ask. Under Chapter 119, Florida Statutes, you can request records in person, by phone, email or letter, and you don't have to explain why. The law doesn't require your name, but when there's a charge the office needs a way to send the estimate, collect payment and deliver the records, so this form includes it. Costs. Agencies may charge for copies (usually 15 cents a page) and, for requests that take extensive staff time, a special service charge. The request asks them to tell you before running up a charge. Exemptions. If they hold something back, they must tell you which law exempts it and release the rest. Help this site. If you get records that fill a gap here, send them in and we'll add them with credit to the public record. The office replies to you. The letter says it was prepared on BayCounty.me, and asks that every reply, cost estimate and record go directly to you. BayCounty.me doesn't receive anything. This page writes the request; it doesn't send it or keep a copy. Nothing you type here is stored.

Who Runs Bay County Who runs Bay County Bay County has one county government, seven cities, a school district and five independently elected county officers. Here's who holds each seat, who's appointed to run things day to day, and what top officials are paid. Export PDF Data updated Oct 21, 2026 Government All governments Bay County Bay District Schools Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach Bay County includes the five county officers The simple version Who's in charge of what Elected boards set policy and budgets. The County Commission, each city commission or council, and the School Board vote on budgets, tax rates and big contracts. Appointed managers run operations. A county manager or city manager, hired by the board, runs departments and staff. Springfield and Parker have no manager; the board oversees staff directly and a city clerk handles administration. Five county officers are elected on their own. The Sheriff, Property Appraiser, Tax Collector, Clerk of Court and Supervisor of Elections each run their own office. The County Commission funds most of their budgets. Their pay is set by a state formula. Money raised for one purpose, like water bills or a sales tax, goes into its own fund and can only be spent on that purpose. The General Fund is the everyday account. Police, parks, roads and city hall are paid from it, mostly with property tax. Totals count some money twice. When one fund pays another (a transfer), both show it, so totals aren't a perfect measure of size. The notes below say what each total includes. Download: CSV · JSON · all open data How the services are grouped, and what to watch for Departments are grouped by name. Each government names its departments differently, so they're sorted into common services. Hover a bar or read the line under each name to see exactly which departments were added together. Only the General Fund is counted. Some cities pay for a service partly from other funds (a roads fund, a fire assessment, the CRA), so their General Fund figure can understate the full cost. Left out of every service: transfers to other funds, reserves, debt payments and hurricane-recovery (FEMA and debris) lines. "Everyday General Fund" is the General Fund without those. Contract services count too. Callaway and Mexico Beach pay the Sheriff for policing; that contract is their police cost. Visitors raise the numbers. Panama City Beach and Mexico Beach serve far more people than live there, so their per-resident costs run high. Bay County is shown for context only. Its figures are spread over every county resident, though much of the Sheriff's patrol serves unincorporated areas. The school district isn't compared here. Public Money · Exemptions Property tax exemptions Who doesn't pay property tax on part or all of their property, and what it adds up to. From the 2026 tax roll for every parcel in Bay County, with a closer look at exemptions for veterans. Export PDF 2026 tax roll City All governments Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach Homestead and veteran counts follow the city; dollar totals and the tables are countywide The simple version How an exemption works An exemption takes value off the tax bill. A $25,000 exemption means you're taxed as if your home were worth $25,000 less. A full exemption means no property tax at all. Most are set by the Florida Constitution and state law. Local governments choose only a few, like the extra exemption for seniors with limited income. Exempt value spreads the cost. When value is exempt, each tax rate raises less from it, so the rest of the tax base carries more of the budget. The dollars here estimate the tax each exemption takes off the bill at current rates. Public Money · Contracts Who gets the contracts The big contracts Bay County and its cities approved since October 2022: who won them, how they were awarded, which ones grew, and who the county actually paid the most. Export PDF Agendas Oct 2022 to Oct 2026 Data updated Oct 23, 2026 Government All governments Bay County Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach The simple version How a government picks a contractor Big purchases must be bid. Above a dollar limit ($150,000 for the county, $100,000 for Panama City), the government advertises the job and usually takes the lowest qualified bid. Engineers and architects are chosen on qualifications (an RFQ), then the price is negotiated. Many jobs go to firms already under a "continuing services" contract as task orders. Shortcuts exist, with rules. A government can "piggyback" on another government's bid, use a sole source when only one vendor can do it, or buy in an emergency and get approval afterward. Contracts can grow. A change order adds cost or time after signing, and big ones need board approval. Get involved · Correspondence Letters to officials Emails BayCounty.me has sent to Bay County's elected officials and managers, and what they wrote back. Each email goes to one person, never a whole board, so officials can't reply to each other outside a public meeting. Government All governments Bay County Bay District Schools Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach All governments Loading… About these emails They're public records. Under Chapter 119, Florida Statutes, officials' emails about public business are open to anyone. Every email we send says replies may be published here. We show the new part of each reply. Earlier messages quoted at the bottom of a reply are left out, since they repeat what's already shown. Officials are named with their seat; email addresses aren't shown. “No reply yet” means nothing has come back to us. It can take a while, and some answers come by phone or in a public meeting instead. Something wrong? If you're an official and we've misrepresented a reply, tell us and we'll fix it.

Connections · Shared owners One owner, several checks Groups of businesses that list the same officer, manager or registered agent in state corporate records and each gave to the same local candidate. Each group was checked by hand against the state's records before it was listed here. All elections All candidates Loading… Gifts over the $1,000 limit One organization, one candidate, one election Florida limits each contributor to $1,000 per election for a local candidate (s. 106.08, F.S.); the primary and the general each count as their own election. These are cases where a campaign's own reports show more than that from one organization, net of refunds. Each was checked by hand. Open means no explanation has been found yet. Resolved means it was explained (for example a reporting error, an amended report, a refund, a check meant for the general election, or an Elections Commission ruling), and the explanation is shown. Loading… About this list This is legal. Under Florida law each corporation or LLC is its own contributor with its own limit ($1,000 per election for local offices), so one owner's companies can each give. Giving in someone else's name is what the law forbids (s. 106.08(5), F.S.). A group here is a pattern in public records, not a finding of wrongdoing. How businesses are linked. Business contributors in the Supervisor of Elections reports are matched to the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) file. Businesses are grouped when they list the same person as an officer, manager or registered agent, matched by name and address. Corporate officers on 25 or more companies and registered-agent services are left out. Years. Groups are listed by the election the checks were for, newest first. Candidates often raise money a year or more ahead, so checks for a 2024 race can be dated 2023; each card says when its checks were written. Inactive businesses are flagged. A business marked Inactive is dissolved, revoked or no longer filing annual reports with the state; "since" is the last year it filed. Its gift was made while it was still filing. Over the limit. A reported overage is not a finding of wrongdoing. Reports can contain typing errors, a check written before the primary can be meant for the general election, and a campaign fixes an overage by refunding it. Only the Florida Elections Commission decides whether the law was broken. Data: /api/v1/datasets/over-limit-gifts . People aren't named. BayCounty.me doesn't name individual donors. Each business links to its public Sunbiz record. Something wrong? If a business is grouped by mistake, tell us and we'll correct it. The data is also at /api/v1/datasets/shared-owner-groups .

Connections · Nonprofits Bay County nonprofits Every local nonprofit, starting with the ones tied to public money and campaigns. Search for any one, or tap a card. Network Shared owners Nonprofits People More filters All types All cities Include homeowner and condo associations Registered Florida charities only Loading… Show more Pick a nonprofit or a person to see its connections, board, money and filings. Sources and method Which organizations. Every organization the IRS recognizes as tax-exempt with an address in Bay County (the IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File), plus active Florida nonprofit corporations (Sunbiz) whose principal address is in the county. IRS and state records are joined by the EIN the corporation gives the state, then by exact name. Money. Revenue, expenses and assets come from the latest 990, 990-EZ or 990-PF the organization e-filed (2019 on). Small organizations file a 990-N postcard with no figures, and churches don't have to file. Government payment records are the site's contracts, check registers, tourism agency payments and CRA ledger, matched to the nonprofit by name. Grants are from Schedule I of local nonprofits' returns. Florida charity registrations. Charities that ask Floridians for donations must register each year with the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services. The registrations with a Bay County address come from its Check-A-Charity database: status, expiration, the revenue and the program, fundraising and management spending the charity reported, and its professional fundraising firms. Check-A-Charity lists no tax ID, so registrations are joined to the IRS and state records by exact name; 45 match neither and are listed on their own. Officers and directors appear only in the application PDFs each charity uploads and are not included yet. Churches and some small charities are exempt from registering, so a missing registration is not by itself a problem. Board members. 990 and 990-EZ returns list officers, directors, trustees and key employees with their hours and pay; 990-N postcards name a principal officer; the state lists up to six officers. Names are shown as filed and grouped across boards by last and first name (nicknames such as Bob and Robert count as one), so two people with a common name can be grouped together. "Shares board members" counts other local nonprofits whose latest filings list the same name. Businesses come from Florida corporate filings (Sunbiz officers and registered agents): "name and address" means the person on the nonprofit's own state filing is the same Sunbiz person; "name" means only one Sunbiz person in the county has that name. Campaign gifts are the business's own gifts in Supervisor of Elections reports. An "official" tag means the name was checked by hand against an elected official, department leader or candidate. Something wrong? Tell us . The data is at /api/v1/datasets/nonprofits , nonprofit-board-members , nonprofit-board-businesses , nonprofit-payments , nonprofit-grants , charity-registrations and nonprofit-officials . IRS e-file data comes through the GivingTuesday 990 data lake.

Connections · Business ties Officials' businesses The registered businesses and nonprofits that list a Bay County official, department leader or candidate as an officer, manager or registered agent, and where those businesses meet campaigns and public money. Each match was checked by hand against state corporate records. Everyone Only people with links Loading… About this list Where it comes from. The Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) quarterly file lists each company's officers, managers and registered agent. Officials are matched by name, then each match is checked by hand (address, middle initial, the business itself) before it is listed. The bars. Each bar runs from the year the business was filed to today, or to its last filing (usually the dissolution) if it has closed. Sunbiz shows only current officers, so a bar says when the business existed, not exactly when the official joined it. From late 2026 on, BayCounty.me records when each officer first and last appears. Links. Two officials on the same business; an official's business giving to a campaign; a business that gave to a candidate and shares an officer with that candidate's own business (the shared person is counted, not named); and an official's business paid by a local government. A link is a fact in public records, not a finding of wrongdoing. Many are civic nonprofits that officials serve on as part of the job. Only officials and candidates are named. Other people on these businesses are never listed. Something wrong? Tell us and we'll correct it. The data is also at /api/v1/datasets/official-businesses and /api/v1/datasets/official-business-links .

Public Money · Accountability Accountability console Public projects followed from the first budget to the day they close: what was promised, what was approved, every change order and payment we can find, and what it cost in the end. Where the record raises a question, it's flagged by a published rule and sent to the agency for an answer. Government All governments Bay County Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Mexico Beach 94 projects tracked $399.6M in those projects 43 with a question 29 records still missing 0 agency replies How it works Four steps for every project One timeline. Budgets, approvals, contracts, change orders, votes and payments from the site's records are put in order for each project, each with its source. Promised vs. delivered. The first firm figure is compared with the latest, and the planned finish with the real one. Flags follow rules. A flag is raised only by one of the published rules below, the same way for every government. A flag is a question, not an accusation. Agencies get to answer. Flags are sent to the agency, and its reply is posted beside them. Records we're missing become ready-to-send requests . Projects Year All years All governments Bay County Callaway Lynn Haven Mexico Beach Panama City Panama City Beach Springfield Any flag or none Any flag Cost grew more than 10% Running late Figures don't agree Who was paid isn't public yet Local share unclear Budgeted, but spending not shown Approval not found in the minutes More than one incentive, same place Dropped from the schedule All projects Reviewed project histories Contracts with change orders Sales tax projects Most questions first Biggest first Latest activity first Most cost growth Download CSV Loading projects… Show more The flag rules Every flag on this page comes from one of these rules. Each project's flags link back here. If a rule is unfair or applied wrong, tell us . Cost grew more than 10% When it's raised The latest firm figure (final cost, current contract total or current project estimate) is more than 10% above the first firm figure (the award or first budget). Over 25% is marked high. What it means The project costs noticeably more than the public was first told. Bay County and Panama City require board approval once change orders pass 10%. What it doesn't mean It does not mean money was wasted. Scope added on purpose, design and land costs, and price changes all raise totals. The flag asks the agency to explain the difference. Running late When it's raised A source reports the project finished more than 90 days after its schedule, or a sales tax project is not complete after the last year it was programmed for. Over a year is marked high. What it means The public waited longer than planned, which often costs money too. What it doesn't mean Delays are often caused by utilities, permits, storms or grant timing outside the agency's control. Figures don't agree When it's raised Two or more public documents give different amounts for the same project and period. What it means Residents cannot tell from the public record what the project costs or what was spent. What it doesn't mean The documents may count different things (one phase, the CRA share, the whole project). The agency can settle it with one breakdown. Who was paid isn't public yet When it's raised Money was spent or committed, but no record we have names the contractor or seller, or states the price. What it means The public cannot check who received the money or for how much. What it doesn't mean The information usually exists in the agency's files; it just wasn't in the report we read. A records request will usually get it. Local share unclear When it's raised The project mixes CRA or city money with state or federal grants, and no record says how much is local tax money. What it means The totals shown overstate what local taxpayers paid, by an unknown amount. What it doesn't mean Grants are good for local taxpayers. The flag is only about knowing the split. Budgeted, but spending not shown When it's raised A budget was set, but actual spending is under half of it for a year that has ended, or no record of actual spending was found. What it means The money may be sitting unspent, may have been moved, or the work stalled. What it doesn't mean Unspent budgets often roll over to the next year, and a delayed project may still be on track overall. Approval not found in the minutes When it's raised A change order appeared on an agenda, but the meeting minutes we read do not record a vote approving it. What it means We could not confirm the board approved the added cost. What it doesn't mean It may have been approved on a consent agenda, in minutes we have not read, or by staff within their authority. More than one incentive, same place When it's raised One address or company receives more than one grant or rebate from the same agency. What it means The total public support is easy to miss when each award is reported on its own. What it doesn't mean Programs usually allow this. The flag adds it up; it does not say it was wrong. Dropped from the schedule When it's raised A project was struck from the sales tax project schedule. What it means Money promised to voters for this project went elsewhere or is on hold. What it doesn't mean Schedules are amended when costs, grants or priorities change; the replacement project may be listed. Records still missing The questions above can usually be answered from records the agency already keeps. Each one opens a Florida public records request, written and ready to send. Right of reply, and how this was built Before a project's flags are treated as final, the agency is sent the flags and the records behind them, and asked to correct or explain. Its answer is posted with the project, in full or linked. Each project shows where that stands. Reviewed project histories were put together by hand from the CRA ledger, city capital schedules, resolutions and news reports. Contract timelines come from the contracts and change orders on the Contracts page, and votes from How They Voted . Sales tax projects come from the county's project schedule and map. News reports are marked as news. When an event's figure comes from a note on a source record rather than the document itself, it says so. Dollar totals add each project's latest figure once. Grants are included, so totals are more than local tax money alone. Download everything as JSON . Corrections: send one .

Accountability · Votes How they voted Budgets, tax rates, big contracts, land deals and borrowing are decided by recorded votes. Here's how each elected official voted on the money decisions since 2024, from official minutes. Export PDF Minutes Jan 2024 to Oct 2026 Data updated Oct 23, 2026 Government All governments Bay County Bay District Schools Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach The simple version Reading the votes Most votes are unanimous. A bond or loan pays for something big today, like a water plant or a building, and gets paid back with interest over years. Each debt names its money source. Most local debt here is repaid from a specific stream (sales tax, utility bills, tourist tax) rather than from a property tax voters approved. That's why almost none of it is "general obligation" debt. Most of it is bank loans. In Bay County, nearly all borrowing is placed directly with banks or the state, not sold to the public as bonds. Pensions are a separate promise. Money owed to employees' future pensions and retiree health care is listed separately; it isn't borrowing, but it's still owed. Glossary Plain-English guide Government money comes with a lot of jargon. Here is every term on this site, explained simply first, with more detail after. Anywhere on the site, a word with a dotted underline can be tapped for its short explanation. Community Redevelopment Agencies Property taxes and your bill Budgets and where money comes from How we label spending on this site Contracts, land and borrowing Public records Community Redevelopment Agencies Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) A savings jar for one neighborhood that needs fixing up. When the neighborhood's property gets more valuable, the extra tax money goes into the jar, and it can only be spent in that neighborhood. Florida law lets a city or county create a CRA for an area it officially finds run-down. The city commission usually acts as the CRA's board. It follows a written redevelopment plan and has an end date. Example: Lynn Haven's CRA covers about 695 acres around Ohio and Florida Avenues. CRA district The line drawn on the map around the neighborhood a CRA covers. Money raised inside the line is spent inside the line. Some CRAs have several districts. Panama City has four: Downtown, Downtown North, St. Andrews and Millville. Tax increment (TIF) The extra property tax a neighborhood brings in because its property became worth more after the CRA started. That extra is what fills the CRA's jar. On the day a CRA starts, the total property value inside it is written down. Every year after, the city and the county each pay into the CRA's trust fund the taxes on any value above that starting number. TIF stands for tax increment financing. Example: If a district was worth $100 million when it started and is worth $150 million now, the taxes on the $50 million difference go to the CRA. Base year The starting snapshot of how much all the property in a CRA was worth. Only growth above this number pays into the CRA. The base year is set when the CRA is created and stays the same for the life of the CRA. CRA trust fund The CRA's own bank account. Tax increment goes in, and by law it can only be spent on that CRA's plan. State law (Chapter 163, Part III) requires each CRA to keep its money in a separate trust fund and report how it was spent every year. Sunset date The day a CRA is scheduled to end. After that, the extra tax money goes back to the city and county budgets. A city can vote to extend a CRA's life. Lynn Haven extended its CRA to 2043 in January 2026. TIF rebate A deal where the CRA gives a builder back part of the new taxes their project creates, for a set number of years, to help get the project built. The rebate is paid only after the owner pays the full tax bill, and it has a maximum amount. Example: Panama City approved five TIF rebate awards downtown in December 2024. Façade or storefront grant Money a CRA gives a business owner to fix up the front of their building, usually matching what the owner spends. Most programs are 50/50: the CRA pays half, up to a limit, after the work is done. Property taxes and your bill Property tax (ad valorem tax) A tax based on what your house or land is worth. More valuable property pays more. Ad valorem is Latin for 'according to value.' Several governments each charge their own property tax, and all of them show up on one bill from the Tax Collector. Taxing authority Any government allowed to put a property tax on your bill, like the county, the school board or your city. Each one sets its own rate every year at a public hearing. Millage (mills) How property tax rates are written. One mill means $1 of tax for every $1,000 your property is taxed on. A rate of 5.5 mills is the same as 0.55%. Your bill adds up the mills from every taxing authority that covers your address. Example: 5 mills on a home taxed at $200,000 is $1,000 a year. Just value The Property Appraiser's estimate of what your property would sell for. It is set as of January 1 each year. Assessed value Your property's value after any limits on how fast it can go up. For a homestead, it usually rises more slowly than the market. Florida's Save Our Homes rule keeps a homestead's assessed value from rising more than 3% a year, or the rate of inflation if lower. Taxable value The number your tax is actually figured on: the assessed value minus any exemptions. It can be different for school taxes and other taxes, because one homestead exemption does not apply to school taxes. Homestead exemption A discount on property taxes for the home you live in full time, as long as you apply for it. The first $25,000 of value is exempt from all property taxes. A second amount, on assessed value above $50,000, is exempt from every tax except school taxes. It was $25,000 until 2024 and now rises with inflation: $25,722 in 2025 and $26,411 in 2026. Example: In 2025, a homestead assessed at $200,000 was taxed on $149,278 by the city and county and on $175,000 by the school board. Rolled-back rate The tax rate that would bring in the same money as last year from the same properties. If a government picks a higher rate, the law calls it a tax increase, even if the rate didn't change. New construction is left out of the calculation, so growth alone does not count as an increase. TRIM notice The postcard you get each August showing your proposed taxes and when the public hearings are. TRIM stands for Truth in Millage, Florida's law that sets the steps governments must follow before raising property taxes. Non-ad valorem assessment A flat fee on your tax bill for a service, like garbage pickup or fire protection. It isn't based on what your property is worth. It appears on the same bill as property taxes but is calculated per home, per acre or per unit instead of by value. MSTU An extra county tax area that pays for services in only part of the county, usually the areas outside cities. MSTU stands for Municipal Service Taxing Unit. Required Local Effort The school tax rate the state tells every school district to charge so it can get its share of state school money. The Legislature sets it each year. School boards can add a small discretionary rate and a capital rate for buildings. Save Our Homes cap A limit on how fast a homestead's taxed value can go up: 3% a year, or less if inflation is lower. Rentals, businesses and second homes have a looser 10% limit. The limits apply to assessed value, not to tax rates. Amendment 3 would lower the 10% limit to 5% for non-school taxes. Levy The total property tax a government collects in a year: its rate times all the taxable value in its area. Budgets and where money comes from Revenue Estimating Conference The state's team of economists that estimates how much money a new law or amendment would add or take away. Staff from the Legislature, the Governor's office and the Office of Economic and Demographic Research agree on one official estimate. Example: For Amendment 3, it estimated the loss for every county, city and special district. Fiscal year (FY) A government's budget year. In Florida it runs from October 1 to September 30. It is named for the year it ends in. Example: FY2026 runs from October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026. General fund A government's main checking account for everyday services like police, parks and running city hall. Most property tax goes here. Money for special purposes is kept in separate funds. Enterprise fund An account for a service you pay for directly, like water and sewer. The bills you pay cover the service. These run like a small business inside the government. Special revenue fund Money that by law can only be spent on one thing, like gas tax for roads or a CRA's trust fund. State shared revenue Money the state collects, mostly from sales tax, and sends back to cities and counties. The biggest piece is the half-cent sales tax program. Cities and counties also get revenue-sharing money based on population and other factors. Charges for services Money a government earns by charging for things it provides, like water bills, garbage pickup, permits and park fees. Intergovernmental revenue Money one government gets from another, like federal grants or state shared revenue. Constitutional officers The elected county officials named in Florida's constitution: the sheriff, property appraiser, tax collector, clerk of court and supervisor of elections. Each has its own budget, and the county pays for most of them. Audit / annual financial report A yearly check of a government's books by outside accountants, to make sure the numbers add up and the rules were followed. Florida governments must file their audits and financial reports with the state. This site uses those filings. How we label spending on this site Spent The record says the money was actually paid out. Committed A contract or award has been approved, but not all of the money has been paid yet. Budgeted Money set aside in a plan. It may or may not be spent. Proposed An idea or request that hasn't been approved. Left out of totals Shown on the site, but not added into the totals, so the same dollar is never counted twice. Examples: a change order that is already part of a project total, a possible duplicate, or money that isn't from the CRA. Contracts, land and borrowing Change order An approved change to a contract after it is signed, which often adds cost or time. Right-of-way The land a road sits on plus the strip alongside it for sidewalks, utilities and drainage. Widening a road often means buying more right-of-way. Eminent domain When a government buys private land for a public project even if the owner doesn't want to sell. A court decides the fair price. The court process is called condemnation. Bond A way for a government to borrow money now and pay it back with interest over many years, like a mortgage. The yearly payments are called debt service. Community Development District (CDD) A special government created for one development to build and pay for its roads, pipes and other basics. The property owners there pay for it. Interlocal agreement A contract between two governments, like a city and the county. Public records Public records request Asking a government to show you or send you its records. In Florida, anyone can ask, and you don't have to say why. Florida's public records law is Chapter 119 of the Florida Statutes. Governments can charge for copies and for large amounts of staff time. Check register A government's list of every payment it made: who got paid, how much, when and for what. It is the most direct way to see where money went, and most cities don't post it online.

About About BayCounty.me BayCounty.me is an independent project that collects Bay County, Florida public records and turns them into maps and tables anyone can read. It starts with how local governments spend public money and will grow from there. Where the information comes from Everything on the site comes from documents the public can already request or download: city and county budgets, annual reports, audits filed with the Florida Auditor General, council and commission resolutions, Bay County GIS map layers, and reporting by local newsrooms. Each figure carries a link to its source. What the labels mean Spent : the record reports the money as paid. Committed : a contract or award has been approved but is not fully paid. Budgeted or Proposed : a plan or appropriation, not a payment. Totals count each dollar once. When one record is part of another (a change order inside a project total, for example), it stays visible but is left out of the totals. Corrections, records and questions Found an error, or have a public record that fills a gap? Send it here. Corrections are dated on the page they affect and listed under What's new . Privacy BayCounty.me doesn't sell, share or track you. There are no accounts, no ads and no tracking cookies, on the website or in the iPhone app. The website Visits. The site counts page views with Vercel Web Analytics, which uses no cookies and doesn't identify you. Email alerts. If you sign up, we keep your email address and what you chose to follow, so we can send the emails. Every email has a link to change or stop them. To have your address deleted entirely, email us. Contact form. Your message, name and email come to us by email so we can answer. They aren't added to any list. API. Requests to the public API are logged with the caller's IP address for 90 days to stop abuse, then deleted. My Address. Address lookups go straight from your browser to Bay County's and FEMA's public map servers. BayCounty.me doesn't receive or store what you look up. The iPhone app No data collected. The app has no accounts, analytics or advertising, and sends nothing about you to BayCounty.me. Your address and location. If you save a home address, it stays on your phone. If you tap "Use my location," the app asks permission first and uses your location once to find your address on Bay County's public map server. It isn't stored or sent anywhere else. Downloaded data. The app saves copies of the public records it shows so it works offline. Deleting the app deletes them. Crash reports. If you've allowed it in your iPhone settings, Apple may share anonymous crash reports with the developer. Questions Email hello@fluxlabs.net or use the contact form . BayCounty.me is run by Flux Labs in Panama City, Florida.

Errors or misstatements could go undetected. Budgetary Control Repeat No budget was legally adopted for the Disaster Recovery Fund, even though state law requires spending to follow an adopted budget. Impact Fee Accounting Repeat Impact fees were not kept in a separate fund, as s. 163.31801 F.S. requires. Building Permit Expenditures Repeat Building department spending is not budgeted or tracked separately, so the city cannot show it complies with the state cap on carrying forward building permit fees (s. 553.80(7)(a) F.S.).
